title: Movement of Robots
statement:
Robots sit at distinct integer points of an infinite number line: robot `i` starts at `nums[i]` and, once started, travels one unit per second in the direction `s[i]` (`'L'` toward negative numbers, `'R'` toward positive numbers). Whenever two robots are at the same point at the same instant, both turn around on the spot and keep moving at the same speed. Such a meeting can happen halfway between two integers: a robot at `0` heading right and a robot at `1` heading left meet at `0.5` after half a second, so one second later they are back at `0` heading left and at `1` heading right.

After exactly `d` seconds, take the distance between the two robots of every unordered pair (each pair counted once) and return the total of these distances modulo `10^9 + 7`.
constraints: All values in nums are distinct
signature: int sumDistance(int[] nums, String s, int d)
notes:
## Intuition

Simulating every bounce is hopeless when `d` reaches `10^9`. The trick is that robots are interchangeable for this question: when two of them meet and turn around, the picture is exactly the same as if they had walked straight through each other and swapped names. The answer only depends on the set of final positions, not on which robot stands where, so every robot can be treated as a ghost that ignores collisions and ends at `nums[i] + d` or `nums[i] - d`.

What is left is the classic "sum of all pairwise distances" over a list. After sorting, the element at index `i` is at least as large as the `i` elements before it, so its distances to them add up to `i * value - (sum of those elements)`.

## Approach

1. Move every robot `d` units in its own direction, ignoring collisions, giving `positions`.
2. Sort `positions` numerically.
3. Walk left to right with `prefix` holding the sum of the earlier positions.
4. For index `i`, `gain = i * positions[i] - prefix` is its total distance to all earlier robots; add it to `answer` modulo `MOD`.
5. Add `positions[i]` to `prefix` and continue; return `answer`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [-2, 0, 2]`, `s = "RLL"`, `d = 3`. Ignoring collisions the robots end at `1`, `-3` and `-1`; sorted, `positions = [-3, -1, 1]`.

- `i = 0`: `gain = 0 - 0 = 0`, `prefix = -3`.
- `i = 1`: `gain = 1 * (-1) - (-3) = 2`, `answer = 2`, `prefix = -4`.
- `i = 2`: `gain = 2 * 1 - (-4) = 6`, `answer = 8`.

The result is `8`, matching the bounced positions `[-3, -1, 1]` from the real simulation.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n), dominated by the sort; the scan is linear.
- Space: O(n) for the final positions.

## Pitfalls

- The real total can be around `10^19`, past exact integers in JavaScript and past 64-bit range, so reduce after every `gain` instead of at the end.
- Final positions reach `±3 * 10^9`, beyond 32-bit `int`; Java and C need `long` for positions, `prefix` and `gain`.
- `Array.prototype.sort` compares as strings by default; pass `(a, b) => a - b`.
- Each `gain` is non-negative because the list is sorted, so `%` never produces a negative remainder here.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | the modulus `10^9 + 7` |
| `positions` | where each robot ends if collisions are ignored, then sorted |
| `answer` | running total of distances, modulo `MOD` |
| `prefix` | sum of `positions[0..i-1]` |
| `i` | index of the current position in sorted order |
| `gain` | total distance from `positions[i]` to every earlier position |

narration.3: Treat bounces as robots passing through each other: each one simply ends d units away in its own direction.
narration.4: Sort the end points numerically so every earlier point is to the left of the current one.
narration.6: The running total of distances starts at zero.
narration.7: prefix will hold the sum of all positions before index i.
narration.8: Visit the end points from left to right.
narration.9: The current point is at least as far right as the i points before it, so its distances to them sum to i * value minus their sum.
narration.10: Add that contribution and reduce it modulo MOD right away so the number stays exact.
narration.11: Include the current point in the prefix sum for the points that follow.
narration.13: Every pair has been counted exactly once; return the total.
